hints: Break P into four regions to inspect separately, the two $\text{-CN}$ ends, the central $\text{C=C}$, the $\text{Cl}$ attached to the ring, and the six membered ring itself.
Recall the Cambridge names for a $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ group, a $\text{C=C}$ double bond, a halogen substituent, and a delocalised six membered hydrocarbon ring.
walkthrough:
Spot the nitrogen containing groups**
Look at the right hand end of P. You have two $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ groups attached to the same carbon. That $\text{-CN}$ unit is the nitrile group, sometimes called cyano. Both count as the same functional group type.

Spot the carbon carbon unsaturation**
In the middle you have $\text{CH=C}$. That is a carbon carbon double bond joining the benzylic carbon to the dinitrile carbon. A $\text{C=C}$ that is not part of a benzene ring is an alkene.

Describe the left hand side correctly**
On the left you have a benzene ring with a $\text{Cl}$ directly attached to it. So you have two more descriptors: the delocalised ring is benzene / arene, and the $\text{Cl}$ substituent is chloro, in this case an aryl chloride.

Final answer: Functional groups: nitrile (cyano, $\text{-CN}$) and alkene ($\text{C=C}$).
Chloro (aryl chloride) and benzene ring / arene.

hints: Focus on the $\text{CH=C(CN)}_{2}$ part and picture what happens when the pi bond of the $\text{C=C}$ opens to form two new single bonds to neighbours.
Check whether any small molecule is lost when an alkene polymerises, and remember to show the chain continuing with bonds through the outer carbons for two linked units.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond**
Polymerisation here uses only the alkene $\text{C=C}$. Imagine the pi bond breaking. Each alkene carbon then gains one new sigma bond to the next monomer. The $\text{2-chlorophenyl}$, $\text{H}$ and two $\text{CN}$ groups all stay attached to their original carbons, they just become saturated.

Build two units linked head to tail**
One monomer becomes $\text{-CH(Ar)-C(CN)}_{2}\text{-}$ where $\text{Ar}$ is $\text{2-chlorophenyl}$. Join two of these together: $\text{-CH(Ar)-C(CN)}_{2}\text{-CH(Ar)-C(CN)}_{2}\text{-}$. Draw all single bonds in the backbone and put short continuation bonds through the leftmost and rightmost backbone carbons to show the chain continues.

Name the type**
No atoms are lost, no $\text{HCl}$ or water is given out, the monomer simply adds to the chain by opening $\text{C=C}$. That is addition polymerisation, characteristic of alkenes.

Final answer: Polymer section: $\text{-CH}(2\text{-chlorophenyl})\text{-C(CN)}_{2}\text{-CH}(2\text{-chlorophenyl})\text{-C(CN)}_{2}\text{-}$ with continuation bonds at each end, single bonds only, two repeat units shown.
Type of polymerisation: addition (polymerisation).

hints: For excess $\text{Br}_{2}(\text{aq})$, decide which functional group reacts fastest at room temperature and what adds across the $\text{C=C}$.
For excess hot concentrated acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}(\text{aq})$, recall that vigorous oxidation cleaves the $\text{C=C}$ completely and oxidises an aryl side chain to $\text{-COOH}$.
Think about what fragment the $\text{C(CN)}_{2}$ carbon becomes after $\text{C=C}$ cleavage and strong oxidation, for example ethanedioic acid $\text{HOOC-COOH}$.
For excess hot $\text{HCl(aq)}$, ask which group hydrolyses in hot aqueous acid while the $\text{C=C}$ and arene stay intact.
Write the hydrolysis change $\text{-CN}$ to $\text{-COOH}$ and apply it to both nitrile groups without touching the $\text{CH=C}$ linkage.
For excess $\text{H}_{2}$ with Pt, list all unsaturated centres that can add hydrogen, the $\text{C=C}$, the benzene ring, and the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bonds.
Recall the hydrogenation products, $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{CH}_{2}\text{-CH}$, benzene to cyclohexane, and $\text{-CN}$ to $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$.
Match each reagent to its reaction type vocabulary, addition, oxidation, hydrolysis, reduction or hydrogenation.
walkthrough:
Add bromine across the double bond**
$\text{Br}_{2}$ does electrophilic addition to the isolated $\text{C=C}$. The pi bond breaks and one $\text{Br}$ joins each carbon: $$(2\text{-Cl-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4})\text{-CH=C(CN)}_{2} + \text{Br}_{2} \rightarrow (2\text{-Cl-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4})\text{-CHBr-CBr(CN)}_{2}$$ The arene, $\text{-CN}$ and $\text{Ar-Cl}$ do not react under these mild conditions. Reaction type is (electrophilic) addition.

Cleave with vigorous manganate oxidation**
Hot concentrated acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ is a very strong oxidiser. It cleaves the $\text{C=C}$ completely. Think of cutting the molecule at the double bond and oxidising each cut end to the highest oxidation level. The benzylic side $\text{Ar-CH=}$ becomes $\text{Ar-COOH}$, so you get 2-chlorobenzoic acid, $(2\text{-Cl-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4})\text{COOH}$. The $\text{=C(CN)}_{2}$ fragment is oxidised to ethanedioic acid $\text{HOOC-COOH}$ (oxidised forms of the dinitrile diketone are also accepted). Reaction type is oxidation.

Hydrolyse nitriles with hot aqueous acid**
Hot aqueous $\text{HCl}$ hydrolyses nitriles: $$\text{-C}\equiv\text{N} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{-COOH} + \text{NH}_{3} \text{(as } \text{NH}_{4}^{+}\text{ in acid)}$$ Both $\text{-CN}$ groups on the same carbon change to $\text{-COOH}$, while the $\text{C=C}$, arene and $\text{Ar-Cl}$ survive. Product is $(2\text{-Cl-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4})\text{-CH=C(COOH)}_{2}$. Reaction type is hydrolysis.

Hydrogenate everything unsaturated with excess $\text{H}_{2}$/Pt**
Pt catalyses addition of hydrogen to pi systems. With excess reagent all three types react. The alkene $\text{CH=C}$ becomes $\text{CH}_{2}\text{-CH}$. The benzene ring becomes a cyclohexane ring, giving 2-chlorocyclohexyl, the $\text{Cl}$ remains. Each nitrile is reduced fully: $$\text{-C}\equiv\text{N} + 2\text{H}_{2} \rightarrow \text{-CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$$ So both $\text{-CN}$ become $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$. Overall product: $(2\text{-chlorocyclohexyl})\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH(CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2})_{2}$. Reaction type is reduction, also called hydrogenation.

Final answer: With excess $\text{Br}_{2}(\text{aq})$: $(2\text{-Cl-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4})\text{-CHBr-CBr(CN)}_{2}$, Br on each former alkene carbon; (electrophilic) addition.
With excess hot conc. acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}(\text{aq})$: 2-chlorobenzoic acid, $(2\text{-Cl-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4})\text{COOH}$ plus $\text{HOOC-COOH}$; oxidation.
With excess hot $\text{HCl(aq)}$: $(2\text{-Cl-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4})\text{-CH=C(COOH)}_{2}$, both $\text{-CN}$ to $\text{-COOH}$, $\text{C=C}$ retained; hydrolysis.
With excess $\text{H}_{2}$/Pt: $(2\text{-chlorocyclohexyl})\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH(CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2})_{2}$, alkene and arene saturated and both $\text{-CN}$ to $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$; reduction / hydrogenation.
